THE ORDER AGREED THE SAME NIGHT, AFTER v0.77.0:
(1) rmcp 3.5.0 + the lock refresh + base64, with the deliberate protocol-version choice;
(2) the Actions majors, proven with a release dry run before merge;
(3) the rocksdb change on its own, stopping before flo2.io.
Reasons: (1) is mostly patch-level and one deliberate protocol step. (2) changes only the release machinery, which a dry run now exercises end to end. (3) is the storage engine under every design, so it goes alone and is gated on compatibility.

2026-10-01, LATER — ROUTE CONFIRMED, AND THE SWITCH SIZED. Anthony pointed at the workspace Cargo.toml's own note. It says absorbed verbatim at 0.24, "`rust-rocksdb` (0.52) is the maintained one and is where this should end up … The switch gets its own PR". MEASURED the same night:
- crates.io: rust-rocksdb 0.53.0 (2026-09-05), built on rust-librocksdb-sys 0.48.1+11.8.1, so RocksDB C++ 11.8.1. reflow2 locks rocksdb 0.24.0 on librocksdb-sys 0.17.3+10.4.2, so RocksDB C++ 10.4.2. The switch is therefore also a MAJOR C++ engine step, 10.4 → 11.8. The Cargo.toml note's "(0.52)" is one release stale.
- In the code: the rocksdb crate is used in exactly ONE file on origin/main 64b145a, through Direction::Forward, WriteBufferManager, Cache::new_lru_cache and AsColumnFamilyRef. The API surface to port is small.
- The risk is not the code. It is the on-disk format and rollback. A store opened and written by RocksDB 11.8 may not be readable by 10.4 (today's 0.76.0/0.77.0) if newer defaults change the file format. So the PR must prove two things:
  (1) copies of real stores (reflow2's own ~6k-node design, and a copy of a flo2-hosted design) open under the new build with identical node and edge counts and content hash;
  (2) whether a store written by the new build still opens under 0.77.0.
  If (2) fails, rolling flo2.io forward is one-way, and needs a fresh off-site backup and Anthony's explicit word before deploy.","subject_id":"dec:idea-one-place-to-bump-a-dependency","valid_from":"2026-10-01"}
